Learn verbs together with their fixed preposition and the case it takes.
Ask about things with wo(r) + preposition (Worauf? Woran? Wovon?).
Ask about people with preposition + wen / wem (Auf wen? Mit wem?).
Replace a thing with da(r) + preposition (darauf, daran, davon).
Use “darauf, dass…” and “daran, dass…” to link clauses.
It's a November evening. Mara and Lena are waiting at BER airport. Andrei is coming for a week, following his sister's advice. The plane is delayed.
How much longer do we have to wait? The plane is already forty minutes late.
Who are you actually waiting for? The plane or my brother?
Very funny. I'm waiting for the plane, of course. Andrei just happens to be on it.
Of course. And what do you keep thinking about? You look at the board every two minutes.
I'm thinking about what to say to him. We've talked about everything on the phone. Except one thing.
About what we actually are. I'm a bit afraid of it. What happens if he's only coming as a friend?
Lena. My brother has dreamt of nothing but you for two months. He's even learned German. He asked me for advice. Believe me, he's not coming as a friend.
He asked you for advice? About what?
About being here today. I'm not saying any more. Look, on the board! “Landed”!
Oh God. How do I look? Have I got flour on my face?
Just a little. On your nose. He'll get used to it.
for what, on what (“worauf wartest du” = what are you waiting for)
“sich gewöhnen an” = to get used to
“worauf” = “vo-ROWF”, “darauf” = “da-ROWF”: the stress falls on the preposition.
Many German verbs come with a particular preposition, which often does NOT match the English one. They have to be learned together, along with the case:
Ich gewöhne mich an das Wetter.
I'm getting used to the weather.
Sie nimmt an dem Kurs teil.
She takes part in the course.
“warten auf” = to wait FOR (not “für”!): “Ich warte auf dich” = I'm waiting for you. “denken an” = to think OF / ABOUT, not “denken von”.
When you ask about a THING, you use wo + preposition (with -r- if the preposition starts with a vowel). When you ask about a PERSON, you use preposition + wen / wem:
Worauf wartest du? — Auf den Zug.
Auf wen wartest du? — Auf Andrei.
Woran denkst du? — An die Prüfung.
An wen denkst du? — An meine Mutter.
Wovon träumst du? — Von einem Haus.
Von wem träumst du? — Von Lena.
Womit fährst du? — Mit der U-Bahn.
Mit wem fährst du? — Mit Mara.
wo + r + vowel: worauf, woran, worüber, worum. wo + consonant: wovon, wofür, womit, wozu, wonach.
To avoid repeating a thing, you use da(r) + preposition (only for things, not for people!):
Are you waiting for the bus? — Yes, I'm waiting for it.
Are you thinking about the exam? — Yes, I often think about it.
Are you waiting for Andrei? — Yes, I'm waiting for him. (person → auf ihn, not darauf)
When the “object” of the verb is a whole clause, you put da(r)- + preposition, then “dass” or a question word:
I'm looking forward to Andrei coming.
I'm thinking about what to say to him.
We talked about when we'll get married.
In everyday speech, the “da-” part is often left out: “Ich freue mich, dass du kommst.”
I often think of my family.
She dreams of a house by the sea.

Andrei was the last to come through the gate, with a far too big rucksack and a plastic bag in which three jars of honey were clinking. He saw Lena, stopped and smiled so broadly that Mara knew: her advice had been good. Lena didn't run towards him. She stood there, with flour on her nose, and waited for him to come to her. He came.

Mara looked discreetly at the arrivals board and suddenly became very interested in the flights from Istanbul. When she turned round again, Lena was holding the honey and Andrei had flour on his nose.

On the S-Bahn home they talked about everything and nothing. About the flight, about the weather in Sibiu, about how Mara's mother had got used to her son practising German every evening. “She asks about you every day,” Andrei told Lena. “She wants to know if you're eating enough.” Lena laughed. They still hadn't talked about that one thing. But suddenly it didn't seem important any more.

Andrei stayed at Mara's, on the sofa. On the first evening they all sat at Ludwig's, under the yellow lamp. Ludwig wanted to know everything about Mara's father's bees. He asked about the honey, the flowers, the winter. Andrei answered in German, slowly, with mistakes, but he answered. Ludwig listened carefully and corrected him only once: “Not «ich denke auf dich». «Ich denke an dich». You should remember that, lad. You'll need it often in the next few days.” Lena blushed. They all laughed.

Later that evening Mrs Hoffmann knocked on her living-room ceiling with her stick, which with her meant: come up! Mara took Andrei up to the fourth floor. The old pianist looked him up and down, long and critically, like a teacher before an exam. Then she asked: “You play the guitar, I hear? And you're interested in our baker?” Andrei went as red as a beetroot and just said: “Yes. Both.” Mrs Hoffmann nodded, satisfied. “Good. Honest answers. That's how you recognise good musicians. And good men.” Then she sat down at the piano and asked him to play an old folk song with her on the guitar, one he didn't know. After three minutes he knew it. When Mara and Andrei went back down, Andrei said quietly: “Only special people live here, don't they?” Mara smiled: “You get used to it.”

That night Andrei set his alarm for half past three. In the dark Mara heard him getting dressed quietly, tripping over Fritz, who was sleeping in front of her door, and going down the stairs. She smiled and went back to sleep. She knew where he was going.

At four in the morning Andrei knocked on the back door of the bakery. Lena opened it in her white apron, with her hair pinned up, and looked at him for a long time. “What are you waiting for?” she asked at last. “Come in. The dough won't wait.”

They worked together for two hours, almost without talking. Lena kneaded the bread dough, Andrei shaped pretzels, and this time even the first ones looked like real pretzels. The oven got hot, the windows steamed up, and outside, on Kastanienallee, it was still dark and cold. Emre, Lena's colleague, came at five and stopped in the doorway. Then he turned round and left again. “I'm going to get more milk,” he called. They had plenty of milk.
At six, when the first loaves came out of the oven, they sat down on the flour sacks in the corner, each with a coffee. Lena wiped her hands on her apron and said, without looking at him:
Andrei, we need to talk about it. About us. I'm nine years older than you. I have a bakery in Berlin, you study in Sibiu. One thousand two hundred kilometres. I'm afraid it won't work.

I'm afraid too. But I thought of you every morning for two months. At four. Because I knew you get up at four. I woke up at four, in Sibiu, without an alarm, and thought: now she's kneading the dough. Now she's lighting the oven. Now she's drinking her first coffee.
Lena looked at him. Then she looked at her hands, covered in flour. Then at him again.
So what are you waiting for now?

At half past six the bakery opened, half an hour later than usual. That had never happened in eleven years. The first customers were already waiting outside the door and were surprised: at the delay, at the young man with flour on his face standing behind the counter and saying “Guten Morgen!” in German with a Romanian accent, and at the fact that the baker smiled all morning and counted the rolls wrong twice.

Ludwig came at seven, as he did every morning, with Fritz, to get his two rolls. He looked at Lena, then at Andrei, then at Lena again. He said nothing. He took his rolls, put the money on the counter and walked to the door. There he turned round once more.
Lad, today you've got more flour on your face than on the pretzels. You still need to work on that. But otherwise…
He paused and smiled. “But otherwise I'm very pleased.” Then he went out into the cold November morning, and Fritz barked twice, as if he wanted to say the same thing.
Behind him, in the warm bakery, Lena was counting the rolls for the third time. This time correctly.
